reading.body:
Autonomous response is the dominant capability across this set: five of the six tools act on threats without waiting for human confirmation, which concentrates both power and risk in software that runs continuously and at machine speed.

The tools divide into two functional clusters. Four, CrowdStrike, Darktrace, Palo Alto Networks, and SentinelOne, focus on detecting and responding to threats across networks and endpoints. Okta addresses identity and access, and Zscaler inspects traffic moving through cloud infrastructure. The overlap is meaningful: privileged access management appears in at least two tools, and autonomous response appears across vendors in both clusters, meaning the category is converging on systems that can lock accounts, isolate hosts, or block traffic without a human in the loop.

The jurisdictional split is narrow. Five vendors are US-based, one, Darktrace, is UK-based with a note flagging GDPR relevance. The data does not cover how inference is run, where models are trained, or what compute infrastructure underlies any of these tools, so no claims about grid dependency or data-center footprint can be drawn from it. What the data does establish is that AI with kill-switch and high-privilege capabilities is now a commercial product category, not an experimental one, and that the decision latency these tools eliminate is the same latency that has historically allowed human review.
